scenes.tts: Every pathway in this course has been running in your body the whole time you read it, but at different rates. Many are opposites that could waste energy if both ran flat out in one cell. So the body turns them up and down in a timed sequence, as you move from fed to fasting to starving.
scenes.visual: Pathway chips; glycolysis and gluconeogenesis cancel in a futile cycle; chips resolve into a four-state timeline strip lit in order
scenes.narration: Every pathway in this course has been running in your body the whole time you read it, but at different rates. Many are opposites that could waste energy if both ran flat out in one cell. So the body turns them up and down in a timed sequence, as you move from fed to fasting to starving.

scenes.tts: Watch the hours after a meal and you see a relay, each runner handing blood glucose to the next. Right after eating, glucose floods in from the gut and insulin rises. Liver, muscle, and fat hear: store. The liver lays down glycogen, and muscle takes up glucose. From four to sixteen hours, no more dietary glucose arrives, and glucagon rises. The liver now maintains blood sugar by breaking down its glycogen. That store is finite, and largely gone within about a day. By the end of an overnight fast, making new glucose already supplies roughly as much as glycogen breakdown does.
scenes.visual: Stacked-area plot of where blood glucose comes from over 24 h (diet, glycogen, new glucose) with insulin and glucagon bars

scenes.tts: Next comes fasting, at one to two days. Gluconeogenesis grows as glycogen dwindles. The liver, and more and more the kidney, makes glucose from scratch, drawing on lactate, the amino acid alanine, and glycerol. Meanwhile adipose tissue releases free fatty acids. These become the major fuel for muscle and liver.
scenes.visual: Liver, muscle, adipose chips; lactate, alanine, glycerol flow to liver which emits glucose; fatty acids flow to muscle and liver

scenes.tts: In starvation, the brain is the problem child. It normally burns about 120 grams of glucose a day, and long-chain fatty acids are only a minor fuel. They reach brain tissue, where astrocytes burn some, but neurons rely on other fuels. If glucose were the only option, the body would make all 120 grams by gluconeogenesis. The main raw material would be your own muscle protein. You would consume yourself within weeks.
scenes.visual: Brain with 120 g/day glucose need; fatty acids reach the brain but are barely burned; muscle protein pile drains through liver to supply glucose

scenes.tts: Ketone bodies are the escape. They are small and water-soluble, and they cross into the brain. In starvation, liver ketone production climbs, as the flood of fatty-acid-derived acetyl co-A becomes ketone bodies that are exported. Over days to weeks the brain adapts to burn them, cutting its glucose requirement to roughly 40 grams a day. That protein-sparing effect decides whether you survive a long fast.
scenes.visual: Ketones pass the barrier; glucose need bar shrinks 120 to 40 g; muscle protein pile drains slowly

scenes.tts: The liver makes ketone bodies but cannot use them. It lacks SCOT, the enzyme that reactivates acetoacetate so it can be burned. So everything it produces is shipped out to the brain, heart, and muscle. Ketogenesis is an export business.
